essentials: The regulation **bans products made with forced labour** from being sold in the EU or exported from it, wherever they were made.
It covers **every product and every company**, with no size threshold and no sector list.
It creates **no new due diligence procedure**. Authorities investigate; the burden of proof is on them.

sections.title: Why it exists
text: The International Labour Organization estimates that around 28 million people are in forced labour worldwide. Due diligence laws address company behaviour; this regulation addresses the product itself. If forced labour was used at any stage of extraction, harvest, production or manufacture, the product is to be kept off the EU market.

sections.title: What is banned
text: Forced labour is defined as in the ILO conventions: work exacted under the threat of a penalty and not offered voluntarily, including forced child labour. The ban covers placing a product on the EU market, making it available, including through online sales aimed at EU buyers, and exporting it. It applies to components too: a product is tainted if any part was made with forced labour.

sections.title: How an investigation works
steps: **Leads**: authorities draw on a Commission database of risk areas and products, on submissions through a single portal open to anyone, and on their own information.

**Prioritisation**: cases are ranked by scale and severity, with state-imposed forced labour at the top, by the quantity of products on the market and by how large the tainted share of the product is.
**Preliminary phase**: the authority asks the company what it does to identify and address forced labour risks. A company with credible due diligence may avoid a full investigation.
**Investigation**: if concern remains, the authority investigates, including inspections where possible.
**Decision**: if forced labour is established, the product is banned and must be withdrawn and disposed of. Where the company can show the problem has been eliminated, the decision is reviewed.
after: The lead authority is the Member State's when the suspected forced labour is on its territory, and the Commission's when it is outside the EU. A decision taken in one Member State is recognised in all.

sections.title: What it means for companies
points: There is **no presumption of guilt** by region or sector. Unlike the US law on goods from Xinjiang, the EU regulation leaves the burden of proof with the authorities.
Still, where a company does not cooperate or a foreign government blocks the investigation, the authority may decide on the **available facts**.

The practical defence is **due diligence**: knowing the supply chain and being able to show what was done about risks. The Commission has to publish guidelines on this, including for smaller companies.
A banned product cannot simply be re-exported. It must be **withdrawn and donated, recycled or destroyed**, at the company's cost.
For products of strategic importance to the EU, the authority may order the product to be **withheld** until the forced labour is eliminated, instead of disposed of.

sections.title: Enforcement at the border
text: Customs enforce decisions on imports and exports and can suspend the release of goods. Penalties for ignoring a decision are set by Member States.

mistakes.wrong: The regulation obliges companies to carry out due diligence.
mistakes.right: It contains a product ban and an investigation procedure. Due diligence is the practical way to manage the risk, not a formal duty under this act.
There is no threshold. Size matters only for how authorities prioritise and what they expect.

mistakes.wrong: Products from listed high-risk regions are banned automatically.
mistakes.right: The database guides investigations. A ban requires a decision on a specific product.
It also covers products made in the EU and exports from the EU.

practice: **Map your supply chains** beyond tier 1 for products and regions that appear in the risk database.
**Document** how you identify and address forced labour risks. This is what an authority asks for first.
**Add contractual rights** to obtain information from and audit suppliers.
**Prepare alternatives** for inputs from the highest-risk areas; re-sourcing takes time.
**Name a contact** who can answer an authority's request within its deadlines.

quiz.q: What does the Forced Labour Regulation prohibit?
options: Employing workers from outside the EU
Placing on the EU market, making available or exporting products made with forced labour
Importing from countries without a minimum wage
Sourcing from suppliers without a social audit
quiz.why: It is a product ban covering the EU market and exports, regardless of where the product was made.

options: Companies with more than 1,000 employees
Importers above a volume threshold
All economic operators, regardless of size
Only manufacturers of textiles and electronics
quiz.why: There is no size or sector threshold. Any product and any operator can be affected.

quiz.q: Who has to prove that a product was made with forced labour?
options: The company must prove that it was not
The competent authority
The supplier's government
The consumer who complains
quiz.why: The burden of proof lies with the authorities. There is no presumption based on origin, unlike under the US rules on Xinjiang.

quiz.q: Who leads the investigation when the suspected forced labour takes place outside the EU?
options: The Member State of import
The European Commission
The ILO
The customs authority of the exporting country
quiz.why: The Commission leads for risks outside the EU; national authorities lead for risks on their own territory.

quiz.q: What happens to a product once a ban decision is taken?
options: It may be re-exported to a non-EU country
It may be sold at a discount
It must be withdrawn and donated, recycled or destroyed
It is returned to the supplier
quiz.why: Banned products are withdrawn and disposed of. Export is covered by the ban as well.

quiz.q: From when does the ban apply?
options: 13 December 2024
30 December 2026
14 December 2027
1 January 2030
quiz.why: The regulation entered into force in December 2024 and applies three years later, on 14 December 2027.
